nameStory: The salt marsh moth gets its name from its caterpillars' ability to thrive in coastal salt marshes, where they munch on salt-tolerant plants that would kill most other moth larvae. These hardy little fuzzball caterpillars can handle the salty spray and brackish conditions that make coastal areas so challenging for most insects. It's also called the acrea moth after its scientific name, which honors the species' remarkable adaptability to harsh environments.
description: The salt marsh moth is a medium-sized, cream-colored moth with a fuzzy, robust body and distinctive black spots scattered across its white or pale yellow wings. Adults have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2.5 inches and look somewhat like flying pieces of polka-dotted fabric when they flutter around lights at night. The caterpillars are even more recognizable - they're extremely fuzzy, rust-colored 'woolly bear' type larvae covered in dense, bristly hairs. These moths are part of the tiger moth family, known for their often colorful and patterned wings.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Creamy white or pale yellow wings with scattered black spots that look like someone flicked ink from a pen - the spots are irregular and vary in size across the wing surface

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Very fuzzy, thick body covered in dense white or cream-colored hair that feels soft if gently touched, like a tiny stuffed animal

idTips.label: Caterpillar appearance
idTips.description: Extremely hairy rust-orange to reddish-brown caterpillars with long, bristly hairs that feel stiff and slightly prickly when touched - they curl into a ball when disturbed

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Flies in a somewhat erratic, bouncing pattern at night, strongly attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting where they flutter persistently

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest during the day, holds wings horizontally in a tent-like position over the body, often on vertical surfaces like walls or tree trunks

habitat: Salt marsh moths are found in a variety of coastal and inland habitats throughout New England, from salt marshes and dunes to gardens, fields, and woodland edges. They're particularly common in areas with mixed vegetation including grasses, wildflowers, and shrubs, and their caterpillars feed on an enormous variety of plants from seaside goldenrod to backyard plantains. You'll spot adults around outdoor lights in both rural and suburban areas, especially during warm summer evenings.

seasonality.spring: Young caterpillars emerge from overwintered eggs and begin feeding on fresh plant growth. Adults from the first generation may appear in late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak moth activity with adults commonly seen at lights throughout July and August. Fuzzy caterpillars are most noticeable crawling across sidewalks and roads during their wandering phase in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Late-season caterpillars finish feeding and pupate in preparation for winter. Some adults may emerge for a second generation in early fall before cold weather sets in.
seasonality.winter: Moths overwinter as pupae in cocoons hidden in leaf litter and soil crevices. No visible activity above ground during the coldest months.

funFact: Salt marsh moth caterpillars are basically living garbage disposals - they can eat over 250 different types of plants, including some that are toxic to most other creatures, making them one of the least picky eaters in the entire insect world!
confusionNotes: Salt marsh moths are often confused with other white moths like the fall webworm moth, but salt marsh moths have distinct black spots scattered across their wings while fall webworms are usually pure white or have small dark dots arranged in rows. Remember: scattered ink blots = salt marsh, neat rows or no spots = something else.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they only live in salt marshes, these moths are found far inland and in many different habitats - the name comes from their ability to survive in salty conditions, not their exclusive habitat preference. The 'acrea' in their scientific name doesn't refer to acreage or land area, but is simply part of the species designation given by the original describer.
compareHints: Since salt marsh moths are the only Estigmene species in New England, compare them to other tiger moths in the region. Unlike the more colorful tiger moths with their bright warning patterns, salt marsh moths stick to a simple cream-and-black polka dot theme. They're larger and much fuzzier than most other white moths you'll encounter, and their caterpillars are more densely hairy than other 'woolly bear' species.
